reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Characterised by asymmetric underdevelopment of structures derived from the first and second branchial arches, so facial features are typically lopsided rather than symmetrical
The classic triad comprises epibulbar dermoids or lipodermoids, ear malformations (microtia, preauricular tags or pits), and vertebral anomalies
Mandibular hypoplasia is usually more pronounced on the affected side, producing chin deviation and an asymmetric bite
Hearing loss is common and may be conductive from middle-ear and ossicular maldevelopment or sensorineural, so early audiological assessment is essential
Most cases are sporadic and unilateral, though bilateral involvement with one side dominant is well recognised
Associated anomalies extend beyond the face and can involve the heart, kidneys, and central nervous system, so systemic screening is warranted
Intellect is usually normal, and cognitive concerns often reflect hearing loss or coexisting brain malformation rather than the spectrum itself
reference.pathophysiology: The spectrum is thought to arise from disrupted development of the first and second branchial (pharyngeal) arches and the tissues they give rise to, together with contributions from cranial neural crest cells. A leading hypothesis implicates vascular disruption or haemorrhage in the developing stapedial artery territory early in gestation, leading to variable local tissue loss and hence the striking asymmetry. Because the affected arches contribute to the mandible, external and middle ear, and adjacent facial structures, defects cluster in these regions, while accompanying disturbance of paraxial mesoderm and neural crest migration explains the vertebral, ocular, cardiac, and renal associations. Most cases are sporadic with multifactorial causation.
additionalDifferentials: Treacher Collins syndrome (typically symmetrical mandibulofacial dysostosis)
Townes-Brocks syndrome (ear anomalies with thumb and anorectal defects)
Isolated microtia with hemifacial microsomia (overlapping entity)
Maternal diabetic embryopathy with facial asymmetry
additionalInvestigations: Audiological assessment including brainstem-evoked responses to characterise and quantify hearing loss
Ophthalmological examination to identify epibulbar dermoids, lipodermoids, and eyelid colobomata
Spinal and cervical imaging to detect vertebral segmentation and fusion anomalies
Echocardiography to screen for congenital cardiac defects
Renal ultrasound to exclude urinary tract malformation
Cranial imaging where central nervous system involvement or developmental concern is suspected
redFlags: Neonatal upper airway obstruction from severe mandibular hypoplasia or glossoptosis
Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive requiring nutritional support
Undetected hearing loss threatening speech and language development
Unstable cervical vertebral anomalies posing a risk during anaesthesia or manipulation
Significant undiagnosed cardiac or renal malformation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity and extent of anomalies; many children with milder involvement do well with staged reconstruction and hearing rehabilitation and achieve normal cognition, whereas extensive craniofacial, cardiac, or central nervous system involvement carries greater morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing developmental delay to the syndrome itself rather than to correctable hearing loss
Overlooking the contralateral, less affected side, which frequently has subtle anomalies
Failing to screen for cardiac, renal, and vertebral anomalies because attention focuses on the face
Assuming a genetic recurrence pattern when most cases are sporadic
Neglecting airway assessment before sedation or surgery in infants with mandibular hypoplasia
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
